The Dev-like (OPC) TM was spatially distinct from gliosis-hypoxia, overlapping OPC metaprogram from ref. 15 (Supplementary Fig. 12f). On the basis of state-normalized loadings per factor, we observed modest to high cosine similarity of our TMs to their top matching TMs in the data of ref. 15 (range 0.46–0.92 with global median of 0.69) (Supplementary Fig. 12g), including high similarity of core malignant TMs such as Dev-like (OPC), Dev-like (AC), Gliosis and Hypoxia. These similarities largely recapitulate the stepwise spatial transitions of malignant cell states observed in our study. The differences between the TMs in our work and in ref. 15 included the lack of pial layer TM, rare TMs such as Hypoxic 2 and distinct TAM versus resident Immune niches in the latter. These differences can be explained by anatomical differences between the samples across the two studies as well as the lack of tumour-specific snRNA-seq references for Greenwald Visium data15 precluding further granularity.

We designed three Xenium panels for different applications:

To validate spatial GB architecture across many tumours (n = 17 sections from 8 tumours and 18 tumour sites in total; Fig. 2e, Extended Data Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 14), we supplemented the standard 266-gene Xenium v.1 human brain panel with an extra 49 probes (Supplementary Table 8). The extra custom probes were largely selected by applying a probe selection method, Spapros63, to our snRNA-seq data. Spapros was run without selecting a feature number cutoff (n = none) and default parameters. Malignant and TME cells were run inclusively to ensure useful cell state delineation; however, the atlas was downsampled for each tumour and cell state to reduce the computational burden. We then selected high-quality markers on the basis of the spatial expression according to our Visium data. For each cell state associated with a given marker, we calculated Pearson correlations between the marker voxel expression and cell state abundance inferred through cell2location. Markers with the highest median correlation and strongest inter-tumoural concordance were selected. Markers that were already present in the human brain panel were omitted. This resulted in 44 Spapros-derived cell state markers that were further supplemented by 17 known GB markers, which were expressed in our Visium data. The panel was used on 18 blocks from 7 different patients, on 19 sections in total.

To validate the spatial architecture of fine-grained GB cancer cell states and benchmark cell2location deconvolution on Xenium data (n = 1 section; Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 14), we designed a fully custom Xenium v.1 panel of 460 genes (Supplementary Table 15). Gene selection was guided by cell-type biomarker discovery and functional cell–cell interaction analyses, primarily derived from our snRNA-seq atlas data. We also applied Spapros to refine the panel by selecting genes that jointly optimize transcriptional variation across the targeted fine-grained cell-type subsets.

To quantify GB cell states in GBOs, we supplemented the Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel (1000724) (n = 40 sections from 9 GBOs; Fig. 5) with 100 custom genes (Supplementary Table 16). This add-on panel comprises genes marking the different GB malignant cell states and TME, as well as genes associated with proliferation, developmental neuronal-migration, astrocyte differentiation, ECM remodelling and mesenchymal invasion and stromal-immune programs. Probes for eGFP were also added to track GFP-labelled cells.

For Xenium experiments applying panel 1, default on-instrument nucleus segmentation and expansion was performed on Xenium datasets (Xenium Onboard Analyser versions xenium-1.5.0.3 and 1.6.0.8). Nuclei were segmented from DAPI images, followed by the definition of cell boundary as either a 15 µm expansion or the presence of another cell boundary. For Xenium experiments applying panels 2 and 3, default on-instrument segmentation was performed with multi-tissue staining (Xenium Onboard Analyser version xenium-3.1.0.4 for panel 2 and version xenium-4.0.1.4 for panel 3). After nuclei segmentation with DAPI, cell boundaries were segmented (ATP1A1, E-Cadherin and CD45), followed by defining the cell interior (18S ribosomal RNA (RNA), alphaSMA and Vimentin). In absence of boundary or interior staining, segmented nuclei are expanded by 5 µm or until encountering another cell boundary.

Single-cell Xenium gene expression data were preprocessed using standard Scanpy workflow49. For Xenium v.1 datasets, cell-by-gene matrices were filtered to exclude cells with low numbers of transcripts (total gene count fewer than 10) and genes that expressed in fewer than 10 cells across the dataset. Gene counts were normalized and log-transformed before downstream analysis. Tangram64 (version 1.0.4) was used to transfer coarse cell state labels from our snRNA-seq atlas onto Xenium sections using default parameters. Patient-matched snRNA-seq profiles were used as reference for each Xenium dataset. Intersecting and non-zero expressed genes from both modalities were used as training sets (315 genes). Tangram was trained with default learning rate (0.1) for 500 epochs, in ‘clusters’ mode with a uniform density prior and most probable cell-type labels were transferred to Xenium cells from output mapping. See the section ‘GBO spatiotemporal lineage tracing data analysis’ for the processing and quality control of Xenium Prime datasets.

scFates65 was run independently for each donor. For every donor, cells annotated as AC-progenitor-like, AC-gliosis-like, Gliosis-like or Hypoxic were subset from the raw count matrix; clusters with fewer than 10 cells in that donor were dropped, and donors retaining fewer than two clusters were excluded. Counts were normalized to 10,000 per cell, log-transformed and the top 2,000 HVGs were selected (seurat_v3 flavour), followed by principal components analysis (up to 50 components). To suppress the cell-cycle signal, we computed one-way ANOVA F statistics of each principal component against cluster identity and against cell-cycle phase, and retained only principal components with a cluster F greater than cell-cycle F. Donors with fewer than two such cluster-dominant principal components were excluded. A principal tree was then fitted on this cluster-dominant principal component subspace with scFates.tl.tree (method ppt, σ = 0.1, λ = 10, 50 fitting steps, seed 42), using min(30, max(5, n_cells/100)) nodes to adapt to donor size. The tip with the highest soft-assignment-weighted fraction of AC-progenitor-like cells was set as the root, and pseudotime was computed with scFates.tl.pseudotime. Per-cluster mean pseudotime was then summarized across donors.

We leveraged multiome data to jointly infer subclones from multiome data. For snRNA-seq, we used the inferCNV results described above. For snATAC-seq data, we detected CNs directly on the Cell Ranger ARC ATAC output using epiAneufinder66 with a 1-MB window size and blacklisted regions of hg38 provided by the authors. Cells with total fragment counts of fewer than 20,000 were filtered to ensure sufficient chromosomal coverage.

Clones were called by applying leiden clustering on a neighbourhood graph generated from genome-wide CN calls for each modality. We observed that scATAC-seq-based CNAs showed greater variability than RNA-based CNAs, probably due to the higher sensitivity of ATAC-seq in detecting open chromatin regions, resulting in a larger number of events. To be more conservative and reduce false positives, we matched clones from scATAC-seq to scRNA-seq clones. To reduce clone redundancy, we assessed the similarity between scATAC-seq clones using correlation distance. Clones with pairwise distances below a predefined threshold were merged to eliminate highly similar clones.

To mitigate differences in resolution between modalities, we applied interpolation to the RNA-based copy number variant (CNV) profiles, aligning them with the larger genomic windows of scATAC-seq data. For matching clones across modalities, we computed two metrics: cell overlap and cosine similarity between cluster centroids. Cell overlap was defined as the proportion of cells shared between scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq clones, whereas cosine similarity was calculated on the basis of the mean CNV profile for each clone. These metrics were averaged to create a composite similarity score.

Next, we retained the top 20% of clone matches based on this composite similarity score. For each RNA clone, we greedily selected the most similar scATAC-seq clones, assigning cells shared between matched RNA and ATAC clones to a new joint clone identifier. Finally, we applied label spreading to propagate clone labels to classified RNA cells on the basis of their CNV profiles. Each cell was assigned a probability of belonging to a clone, allowing flexibility in downstream analyses by using different confidence thresholds. For most analyses, we applied a confidence threshold of 0.9 to ensure high-confidence clone assignments. Overall, the methodological concordance with LCM-based WGS orthogonally validated the efficacy of counts-based methods at identifying core clone populations. Furthermore, although there may be minor clones with small artefactual signals introduced by inferential nature of this method, we reasoned that redundant granularity would allow us to conservatively control for genetic heterogeneity when applied to downstream trajectory analyses.

Following sequencing, all low-input WGS data were mapped to the hg38 reference genome using BWA-MEM67. All mutations were called against matched normal blood samples using the Wellcome Sanger Institute variant calling pipeline.

CN variants were called using ASCAT68 and Battenberg69. Battenberg CN results were used for subsequent analyses. For each patient, LCM libraries with sufficient DNA concentrations (10 μg ml−1) and CN diversity were used as the basis for alleleIntegrator27. CNAs were called in the snRNA-seq data using alleleIntegrator. The standard workflow was applied using Battenberg CN segments alongside the standard alleleIntegrator workflow. Clones were identified by first subsetting cells with support for a chr. 7 gain, which is diagnostically relevant to GB, followed by support for putative lineage-specific CNAs (maxPostProb > 0.7).

CaVEMan70 was used to call substitutions. Variants were filtered to account for artefacts consistent with other low-input WGS studies26,44, which involved applying a filter designed to remove false positive variants such as erroneously processed cruciform DNA (https://github.com/MathijsSanders/SangerLCMFiltering). Subsequently, variants were retained if they met a minimum median alignment score of 140 or more, fewer than half reads were clipped (contaminated log-phase multiplier  =0), were supported by at least four variant reads and had a total sequencing depth of 10× or greater. The minimum thresholds for mapping quality and base quality were set to 30 and 25, respectively. Finally, we used a beta-binomial model adapted from the Shearwater variant caller in ref. 71 designed to remove both germline variants and consistently observed low-quality variants. Site-specific error rates were calculated for each variant and only retained if the FDR-corrected P value was less than 0.001. Sample phylogenies were generated using Seqouia72 with default parameters and no application of the binomial mixture model. To ensure Sequoia compatibility with our tumour data, substitutions in CN variable regions were omitted.

Following filtering, PyClone-VI28 was used to cluster variants outside patient-associated CNAs into putative subclones for each patient, separately. Each patient was run with the following non-default parameters: number of grid points 150, number of restarts 100 and number of maximum expected clusters 30. Relationships between inferred clone populations, including phylogenetic analysis, was performed using PairTree73,74 with, apart from default parameters, a burn-in of 0.4 and the RPROP method for fitting subclones to trees. LCM samples were grouped into clusters on the basis of clone population frequencies with agglomerative clustering using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity and complete linkage.

Phenotypic comparisons were performed using adjacent Visium sections. Visium H&E sections were manually annotated with adjacent LCM ROIs through alignment with overlaying adjacent sections. For any spot overlapping with a given LCM ROI, cell state abundances from cell2location were summed to generate ROI-specific cell state distributions. To quantify subclonal diversity in our LCM-WGS data, we used Rao’s Q with a distance matrix corresponding to the cumulative mutational differences between PairTree-defined phylogenetic lineages.

To assess the spatial distribution of multiome-inferred clones (that is, called from joint RNA and ATAC) in Visium data, we developed the SpaceTree model for joint clone and cell state deconvolution (Supplementary Computational Methods). This method follows a multi-step process, beginning with graph construction and followed by the use of a multi-task graph neural network to predict labels for each Visium spot. We used cell2location cell state mapping results to further evaluate the performance of SpaceTree, showing a high degree of concordance (Supplementary Computational Methods, section 2.5.3). Further orthogonal validation of this method was performed through comparison with LCM-derived analyses, including spatial clone cluster concordance (Extended Data Fig. 5g). SpaceTree was run on each Visium section, individually. Cluster concordance evaluation involved summarizing SpaceTree voxel probabilities that were histologically consistent with LCM ROIs into equivalent ROIs. These were hierarchically clustered using the same methodology as LCM samples (agglomerative clustering with Bray–Curtis dissimilarity and complete linkage). Tumour purity was calculated according to SpaceTree clone mapping results and represents the sum probability of all malignant clones in a given Visium spot. Shannon entropy was calculated on clone probabilities per spot and defined more generally as clonal entropy.

To compare SpaceTree results on GB data to alternative methods, we also predicted clonal abundances in Visium ST data by means of cell2location. To do so, we prepared tumour-specific snRNA-seq reference signatures as described above except that here we separately derived (1) concatenated clone and cell-type annotations (that is, joint cell state × clone) and (2) malignant subclone and TME cell state annotations (that is, malignant clone + TME). We used obtained references to run cell2location on Visium ST data combining samples from each tumour together with following parameters: detection_alpha=20, N_cells_per_location=30 and max_epochs=50000. Predicted clone abundances were compared to SpaceTree predictions; for option A, clone abundances were calculated as marginal sums of cell2location predictions.

Cell fate trajectories were inferred using a Bayesian generative model, cell2fate30 from snRNA-seq data with default parameters. This method infers temporal expression modules resulting from the factorization of RNA velocity data and then applies associated models of gene activation to infer cell-specific time along a trajectory. A key advantage of the Bayesian approach is that this method also returns posterior uncertainty estimates for every parameter, allowing for the evaluation of the confidence of cell state transitions. As input, we generated spliced and unspliced counts using STARsolo75 v.2.7.10a. Cell2fate analysis was run for each tumour clone separately using 10X reaction as a batch covariate, with 20 minimum shared genes and 3,000 HVGs in total. Individual cell2fate runs were evaluated first on the basis of maximum cell-specific time (maximum(Tc) > 20), and then flagged as high-quality if average cell state transition scores exceeded 0.25. To quantify cell state transition scores, posterior distributions of cell-specific times were compared between two cell states, with the score equalling to the percentage of cells in state B that have a greater inferred time than the 90th percentile of cells in state A (Extended Data Fig. 6b,e). For applications involving inter-clonal comparison across tumours, inferred times were minimum–maximum normalized. Before streamgraph visualization of cell states (Fig. 5a), cell counts binned across inferred time were smoothed using a Gaussian kernel to reduce the influence of sparsely populated bins (see Extended Data Fig. 7 for raw cell count histograms). Proliferative states were also merged into their corresponding cell class according to proliferative state subclustering results (Supplementary Fig. 6).

RNA velocity modules were subsequently hierarchically clustered using Jaccard distance of the top 200 genes in each module for the purposes of inter-clone module annotation. The ‘meta’-modules were then manually annotated according to (1) the identity of shared top genes, (2) the results of over-representation analysis of MSigDB signatures for this gene list and (3) enrichment of a given meta-module across malignant cell state annotations. Meta-module markers were compiled by taking the top 50 genes associated with each module, and sorting them by the degree of overlap across all modules in a given meta-module.

Using the standard cell2location workflow and the methods outlined in ref. 30, we also spatially mapped RNA velocity modules from cell2fate for a subset of tumours. Sections were selected if the multiome clone associated with the cell2fate run had a frequency of at least 30% in the associated site of sampling.

Count matrices from CPTAC76 and TCGA77,78 bulk RNA-seq samples were downloaded from the Genomic Data Commons. Samples were aggregated and log-normalized using Scanpy49. Relative expression scores were calculated for each meta-module on the basis of commonly observed top genes (n = 200) and samples were annotated as ‘enriched’ for a meta-module if the expression scores were greater than the 75th percentile. Kaplan–Meier analysis followed by the log rank test were performed using the Python package lifelines79 between meta-modules with early and late inferred times.

FASTQ files were processed using the Parse Biosciences Pipeline (v.1.5.0, Parse Biosciences). Following this, we applied quality control thresholds similar to our snRNA-seq dataset: total UMI > 1,000, gene counts more than 500 and expression less than 99th percentile. Whereas doublet detection was applied with Scrublet, scores remained low (median 0.04) and only 0.05% of the dataset flagged.

We applied a stringent transcript count filter to the cell-by-gene matrices (total counts less than 150). Next, we aimed at identifying GFP+ engrafted cells through the expression of eGFP. Owing to possible off-target probe binding activity, eGFP expression was low-count inflated. The distribution of log-transformed eGFP expression was biomodal, so we modelled cell-area-normalized eGFP counts using a two-component Gaussian mixture model to separate background and reporter-positive cells (Supplementary Fig. 23a). To ensure stringency, we estimated expression thresholds by calculating the minimum values among the eGFP-high component (posterior probability more than 0.9). This resulted in two primary thresholds: eGFP expression more than 32 counts and eGFP counts and/or area greater than 12%.

To harmonize our pre-engraftment Parse-seq data, Xenium GBO data and our cell atlas, we integrated all three modalities with scVI13, using sample, study, and cell-cycle phase as covariates (see section ‘snRNA-seq integration’ for hyperparameters). The model was trained without HVG selection due to the limited size of the Xenium panel. Next, we trained a scANVI model, initialized from this scVI model, to perform label transfer between our atlas and the other modalities. Efficacy of label transfer was then evaluated by means of marker gene inspection (Extended Data Fig. 9c).

To analyse spatial organization of malignant cell states along a periphery-core axis, we first generated a concave hull using Shapely with increased vertices (ratio 0.05) providing reference coordinates to the outer periphery of each organoid. We then calculated the Euclidean distance of each malignant cell to these coordinates. Downstream analysis of distance was minimum–maximum normalized within each organoid tissue section to facilitate cross-sample comparison (Fig. 5e).

We performed two sets of CCC analysis to predict TME-derived ligands targeting receptors expressed on malignant cell states across different dev-like versus gliosis-hypoxia microenvironments, focusing on myeloid signalling.

In step 1, we identified TME cell states spatially colocalized with dev-like versus gliosis-hypoxia malignant cell states from Visium ST data (Fig. 2). These included the entire GB TME including myeloid, vasculature and T cells, and was summarized across all tumours (Supplementary Table 11). We then selected malignant cell states present within dev-like versus gliosis-hypoxia microenvironments per each individual tumour (Supplementary Table 12).

In step 2, we performed CCC analysis using the LIANA+ framework (version 1.2.0)80, which integrates several computational methods and previous knowledge resources into a consensus-based approach to identify ligand–receptor interactions. We used the ‘consensus’ approach, combining five different methods implemented in LIANA+: CellPhoneDB, Connectome, log2FC, NATMI, SingleCellSignalR and CellChat. Consensus scores across these methods were calculated using the robust rank aggregation method81, with an ‘expr_prop’ (filtering criteria based on the proportion of cells per cell type) value of 0.05 and ‘n_perms’ (number of permutations) set to 1,000. Here TME cell states were set as the sources (ligands) and the malignant cell states as the targets (receptors). An expression threshold of 0.05 was applied to filter out ligands and receptors below this threshold. We applied the LIANA analysis separately to the dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia microenvironments.

In step 3, the resulting ligand–receptor pairs were analysed using the Tensor-cell2cell method82 (version 0.7.4), which used the LIANA+ results as input to identify shared CCC events across tumours as factors. This method automatically determined the number of factors using elbow analysis and used robust tensor factorization to ensure consistent results across donors. The main parameters and their values used in this analysis were as follows: ‘score_key = magnitude_rank’ (the LIANA+ score used for factor analysis), ‘tf_optimization = robust’ (the robustness setting for tensor factorization), ‘upper_rank = 15’ (the upper limit for the number of factors) and ‘tf_svd = numpy_svd’ (the singular value decomposition method used). We then identified factors shared across tumours that involve myeloid cells, specifically factors 1 and 2 from the dev-like analysis and factor 1 from the gliosis-hypoxia analysis (Supplementary Fig. 26).

In step 4, we sorted cell interactions associated with each factor on the basis of their loadings and selected interactions in the top 50th percentile. We then focused on ligands from the myeloid populations that are predicted to target receptors on their respective malignant cell states. We filtered the ligand–receptor pair list to ensure at least one relevant cell state showed mean gene expression 0.5 or greater and had a total expression fraction 0.1 or more for each associated gene pair. This resulted in the identification of 80 unique interactions in the dev-like microenvironments (involving 37 ligands), 35 unique interactions in the gliosis analysis (involving 18 ligands) and a total of 63 shared interactions shared across both microenvironments (involving 28 ligands).

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The processed single-cell and spatial atlassing datasets can be explored and downloaded from our interactive webportal (www.gbmspace.org/). The raw sequencing datasets are deposited on the European Genome–Phenome Archive including 10X multiome (accession number EGAD00001015526), 10X Visium (EGAD00001015527), LCM-WGS (EGAD00001016155) and Parse scRNA-seq (EGAD00001016126) datasets. Raw data are available under controlled access to enable appropriate reuse of the data while protecting participant confidentiality. Access can be requested through the Wellcome Sanger Institute electronic data access mechanism (https://edam.sanger.ac.uk/login). Processed sequencing outputs are deposited on ArrayExpress including 10X multiome (E-MTAB-17183) and 10X Visium datasets (E-MTAB-17164), the latter including Visium high-resolution histology images. Xenium spatial transcriptomic data are deposited on the BioImage Archive (S-BIAD2898). This study also used the following resource databases: GRCh38 reference, MSigDB v.2023.1.Hs and v.2026.1.Hs, LIANA+ v.1.2 and its constituent ligand–receptor resources, TCGA-GBM and CPTAC survival and RNA-seq data (accessed 2026). Source data are provided with this paper.

SpaceTree code and tutorials are available at GitHub (https://github.com/PMBio/spaceTree and https://pmbio.github.io/spaceTree/, respectively). Custom code necessary to reproduce the presented data is available at GitHub (https://github.com/BayraktarLab/GBM_space_paper). Scripts for transferring H&E annotations to Visium spots are available at GitHub (https://github.com/cellgeni/OMERO_tools/).

#1422. Sydney FC fans vow to return to the stands after ugly clash with police sparked calls for boycott

Published: 01:23 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 03:07 EDT, 6 November 2026

Sydney FC's active supporter group The Cove will return to the stands for the first time since October's derby, following a bitter dispute over allegations police assaulted a teenage fan and handcuffed supporter leaders before throwing them out.

The group will be back for Friday night’s match against Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park, Sydney, after talks involving the club, NSW Police, Venues NSW and stadium security.

The Cove had threatened to boycott matches after the October 16 derby with Western Sydney Wanderers, accusing police of the 'worst policing standards' in the fixture’s 14-year history and demanding the club defend its fans.

Its return comes amid a broader push for reform, with Football Supporters Association Australia declaring that repeated reviews and weekly discussions with police are no longer sufficient.

The dispute followed a scoreless derby attended by more than 30,000 spectators at Allianz Stadium.

The Cove alleged a 17-year-old supporter was repeatedly slammed into safe-standing rails by police before being struck in the back of the head.

Sydney FC supporter group The Cove will return to Allianz Stadium following a bitter dispute over policing at October's derby

It also claimed two chant leaders, known as capos, were removed from the stadium, while five members of its leadership were handcuffed, pressed against walls and ejected without subsequently being charged.

According to the group's statement, officers later told those leadership members: 'We have nothing to legally charge you with, move on.'

The Cove alleged other supporters were also ejected without justification and accused police of antagonising fans rather than protecting them.

Daily Mail has contacted NSW Police for comment.

The Cove supporters' anger extended to Sydney FC, the APL and stadium officials, whom it challenged to intervene.

'Whilst you may stay silent and not fight for your fans, don't come crying if we don't show up,' the group said.

'Active support isn't a crime. Back your f*****g fans.'

At the centre of the dispute was The Cove's allegation that police ignored established arrangements for supporter marshals to help resolve issues in the stands.

The Cove accused police of bypassing supporter marshals during the October 16 clash with Western Sydney Wanderers

The group claimed marshalls and stadium security were overridden, with officers instead entering supporter bays and taking action without consultation.

'Nobody should be made to feel like a criminal for wanting to passionately support their club,' it said.

Sydney FC initially responded by saying it was investigating the allegations with Venues NSW, the APL and NSW Police.

A joint statement released by the club and The Cove on November 5 said subsequent discussions had produced a commitment to stronger communication, mutual respect and clearer matchday processes.

'All parties have agreed on the importance of active support to football in this country, and all believe passionate, active support and a safe matchday experience must go hand in hand,' it said.

The club thanked The Cove's leadership for its professional engagement, while the supporter group thanked Sydney FC for listening to members and standing alongside them.

The statement welcomed fans back but did not announce findings on the alleged derby incidents or specify changes to police operations.

In a subsequent Instagram post, The Cove said it wanted to ensure there was never a repeat of the round-one incidents.

The supporters will return for Sydney FC's clash with Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park

'We are hopeful that future policing at games will reflect the efforts made by the club, and Cove leadership,' it said.

'We will be monitoring the progress closely over the coming rounds.'

The dispute has also drawn intervention from the FSAA, which says supporters elsewhere in Australia and New Zealand share concerns about excessive police and security actions.

In an open letter published on November 5, the association welcomed Western Sydney Wanderers chairman Paul Lederer's criticism of police treatment of his club's fans.

It said APL leaders shared its frustration, but argued the response needed to go beyond discussions after each incident.

'We are now at the point where reactive reviews and weekly chats with police following regular operational failures on match day are simply insufficient,' the association wrote.

The FSAA said it had recommended structural changes in 2025, including rapid response protocols, measures to prevent supporters being demonised and better communication between authorities and fan groups.

It is now pushing for a framework involving senior league management, clubs, supporter leaders, stadium operators, private security and state police commands.

#1421. Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases1,2. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3,4,5,6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota.

The gut microbiome exhibits large variations in its composition and genetic landscape. Within-species genetic variation underlies strain differences in fitness, metabolic capacities, pathogenicity and other biological properties. Thus, the field of microbiome research is moving towards strain-level or genetic-level dissection of the microbial contributions to human health (Supplementary Information). Structural variations in the gut microbiome have been linked to human body mass index (BMI), bile acid concentrations, the human plasma metabolome and host genetics, thereby identifying bacterial genes involved in glucose metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and biotransformation, and N-acetylgalactosamine utilization3,4,5,6.

However, gut microbial genomes also contain abundant SNVs that can modulate microbial function and host interactions. For example, a SNV in the blc gene of Escherichia coli disrupts the intestinal barrier by decreasing the amount of lysophosphatidylethanolamine, a metabolite that aids remission of inflammatory bowel disease7. In the stomach, a SNV in Helicobacter pylori increases gastric cancer risk by enhancing the proteolytic activity of the serine protease HtrA (ref. 8). In Bacteroides coprocola, SNVs in glycosyl hydrolase genes have been associated with type 2 diabetes9. A SNV-based metagenome-wide association study (SNV-MWAS) in an Israeli population identified BMI-associated SNVs that were replicated in a geographically independent Dutch cohort10. Despite these examples, systematic explorations of the relationships between gut microbial SNVs and host phenotypes have not, to our knowledge, been carried out at phenome-wide scale. Such analyses require large-scale human cohort data with both metagenomic and deep phenotypic data, and they need to overcome a number of technical challenges. For example, microbial species exhibit complex population genetic structures, and these strong lineage effects may lead to false discoveries in association studies if population structure is not properly controlled.

In this study, we compiled shotgun metagenomic sequencing data of 11,831 faecal samples from 5 independent cohorts from the Netherlands and a cohort from Tanzania. Gut microbial genotypes were characterized using GT-Pro11, yielding 12.8 million SNVs in core genomic regions. We further developed a linear mixed-model (LMM)-based analysis workflow that controls for within-species population genetic structure to ensure that SNV–phenome associations detected are independent from the cumulative effect of strain lineage. We then conducted a PheWAS to identify associations between common metagenomic SNVs and 244 host phenotypic and exposure factors, using LMM in each cohort, followed by meta-analysis. In total, we detected 940 independent association signals supported by multiple cohorts that link 39,663 SNVs across 101 species to 69 host phenotypes or exposures, and the full set of results are available in an online catalogue. We also performed protein structural analyses to interpret the biological relevance of these associations.

We compiled faecal metagenomic sequencing data for 11,831 samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 cohorts (Fig. 1). Five cohorts are from the Netherlands—the Dutch Microbiome Project (DMP; n = 7,955)12, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD; n = 1,135, plus 340 followed up after an average of 4 years (designated LLD1 for baseline samples and LLD2 for follow-up samples))3,13, the 500-Functional Genomics Project (500FG; n = 529)14,15, the 1000 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Project (IBD; n = 544)16 and 300-Obesity (300OB; n = 298)15,17—and one is from Tanzania (300-Tanzania Functional Genomics Project (300TZFG), n = 320)18 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). For LLD2 and 500FG, we have additional datasets from some of the same individuals (nLLD2 = 251, nFG500 = 459) with samples processed using both DNA extraction methods19 that allowed us to assess the effect of extraction protocol on SNV profiling and the robustness of microbial genotyping (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1). The extensive phenotypic information for the corresponding samples was also curated and harmonized. We integrated 244 phenotypic and exposure factors (92 binary and 152 continuous or ordinal traits) available in the DMP or in at least 2 other cohorts for analysis (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 2). Among these, 131 phenotypes were available for at least 2 cohorts, whereas 113 were only available for the DMP. Across the whole dataset, the sample size per phenotype ranged from 593 to 11,706 (Supplementary Table 2).

In this study, we integrated whole-genome shotgun sequencing (WGS) data of 11,831 faecal samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts and harmonized 244 phenotype and exposure factors across these cohorts. Two of the six cohorts, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD) and 500-Functional Genomics (500FG), are represented by multiple datasets. n represents the number of faecal samples. LLD contains 1,135 samples collected at the study baseline time point (LLD1) and 340 samples collected for a subset of individuals at a follow-up time point after 4 years that were processed using two DNA isolation kits: 253 by QIAGEN QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (FSK; represented by circled F) (LLD2-FSK) and 338 using QIAGEN AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (APK; represented by circled A) (LLD2-APK). 500FG contains 529 samples that were also processed using the two DNA isolation kits: 517 processed using FSK (500FG-FSK) and 471 processed using APK (500FG-APK). To ensure sample independence in our downstream analysis, we used only LLD1 and 500FG-FSK in this analysis, and the additional datasets (LLD2-FSK, LLD2-APK and 500FG-APK) were used only to carry out technical assessments. We then conducted meta-genotyping for the WGS data from stool samples and generated the gut microbial genotype profile, keeping 12.8 million common biallelic microbial SNVs for the LMM-based SNV-MWAS. SNV-MWAS analyses were conducted separately for the six independent datasets from the six cohorts and then integrated through meta-analysis. Linkage disequilibrium-based grouping was conducted to extract independent signals, and an LMM-based permutation test was used to screen for robust association signals. To provide functional interpretation of SNV associations, we then carried out protein structural analysis. Created in BioRender; Fu, J. https://biorender.com/c1z5z7y (2026).

We genotyped 50,945,657 biallelic SNVs in the core genome of 881 species using GT-Pro11, which conducts reference-panel-based SNV detection using k-mer searching and exact matching. The number of SNVs detected in the DMP was higher than in other cohorts, probably owing to its larger sample size (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). The total number of SNVs detected in at least 1 sample for each species ranged from 1 to 342,230 (mean = 58,131) (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The average density of SNVs in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 32 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1d), which is close to previous reports20. To keep only informative species for downstream analysis, we selected ‘common’ SNVs that were present in more than 10% of samples and had a minor allele frequency (MAF) of more than 5% in at least one cohort. Among the 50.95 million SNVs that were detected, 12,761,497 SNVs were common (Supplementary Table 3). As the distribution of common SNV counts per species was bimodal, with two peaks separated by approximately 1,000 SNVs (Extended Data Fig. 1e), we selected species with at least 1,000 common SNVs, resulting in 433 species with 12,706,564 common SNVs (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Table 4). These 433 species collectively accounted for, on average, 84.3% (s.d. = 9.4%) of the total abundance of the gut microbial community. After filtering, 300TZFG had the highest number of species for analysis (327) and the most common SNVs (7,369,266) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1f–h). The average density of common SNV sites in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 16 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1i). The within-species population structure of the 433 species and the effect of technical factors are described extensively in Supplementary Notes 2 and 3 (Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and Supplementary Tables 5–8). We also pre-calculated the Bonferroni-controlled threshold for study-wide significance by dividing 0.05 by the total number of phenotype–SNV pairs tested (922,497,753), yielding a threshold of 5.42 × 10−11 (Methods).

To understand the functional consequences of SNVs, we annotated genes from reference genomes and predicted the potential functional effect of SNVs on bacterial gene products (synonymous, missense, start or stop codon, and non-protein-coding)21 (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 9). Most SNVs (11,819,660, 93.02%) were located in protein-coding regions, including 9,579,907 (75.39%) synonymous, 2,216,969 (17.45%) missense and 22,784 (0.18%) start or stop codon variants (Fig. 2c). The distribution of the proportion of codon-altering SNVs (missense or start or stop codon SNVs) varied across different bacterial species (Extended Data Fig. 2), reflecting the genetic diversity and evolutionary pressures experienced by these species.

We next performed an SNV-MWAS of 244 factors by linking them to 12 million common SNVs using LMMs fitted separately for each species, phenotype and cohort. These LMMs controlled for population structure by including the species-level between-sample genetic linkage matrix as a random effect. Age, sex, species abundance and clean read count were included as fixed-effect covariates, except in the analyses for age and sex themselves. Given that reference and alternative alleles may coexist within a sample with differing abundances, we encoded gut microbial genotypes as a dosage value ranging from 0 to 1 to represent the frequency of the alternative allele.

Following the per-cohort SNV-MWAS, we conducted a meta-analysis weighted by sample size for the SNV–phenotype pairs available in at least two cohorts to integrate the SNV-MWAS results derived from different cohorts (Fig. 1). This included only the independent datasets—that is, excluding LLD2 and 500FG-APK. This analysis identified 49,346 significant and robust associations that passed the study-wide significance cut-off (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11; Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) and were supported by at least 2 cohorts based on a permutation-based robustness test (cohort permutation P < 0.05 with 999 permutations), with the same association direction. These associations involved 39,663 SNVs of 101 species and 69 phenotypes.

As a resource for further validation and hypothesis generation, we have constructed a catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/) that includes all 49,346 robust associations as well as the suggestive signals that passed the species-wide significance level (species-specific, defined by Bonferroni correction based on the number of tested SNVs within each species; Methods) in the meta-analysis and the largest cohort DMP (see examples in Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5).

Most SNV associations (85.76%) were supported by two cohorts, and 14.24% were supported by three or more cohorts (Fig. 3a). Although all associated SNVs showed a similar ratio of start or stop codon or missense SNVs (17.49%) compared with the background (all common SNVs), six phenotypes were significantly enriched for start or stop codon or missense SNVs (χ2 test P < 0.05): Lifelines protein diet score, on-a-diet behaviour during the past month, thrombocyte count, waist circumference, β-blocker intake and sex (Extended Data Fig. 4). SNVs in the non-coding region may affect gene expression through upstream regulators. For example, variants located approximately 10 bp upstream of the start codon may affect the ribosome-binding site or other elements involved in translation initiation, thereby altering bacterial protein expression22. We further examined the distribution patterns of common and phenotype-associated SNVs in gene upstream regions. The common SNV count showed a drop in −10 bp regions (Fig. 3b), and the ratio of SNVs with at least one association showed an uneven distribution, with a drop at −11 bp and two peaks at −55 bp and −83 bp (Fig. 3c).

As SNVs can be correlated due to linkage disequilibrium in the genomes, we conducted a grouping analysis to select the most significant SNVs within each linkage disequilibrium block as representative tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 < 0.01; Methods). We then identified 940 independent SNV-MWAS signals (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Table 10) and 13,198 SNVs with a high probability of contribution to phenotypic variation (posterior inclusion probability > 0.8) (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Power assessment found that 70.5% of signals have more than 0.80 power to be detected given the observed effect size, sample size, and MAF (Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7) and showed a negative correlation between MAF and effect size (Fig. 3f, R = −0.29, P = 6.06 × 10−20). We also assessed replication across cohorts of different ancestries. Among the 940 signals, 215 had both SNVs and phenotypes available in the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts, with 161 (74.9%) signals involving 8 different phenotypes supported by both cohorts. For example, 48 association signals of 23 species with age are supported by Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Notably, among the 940 SNV–phenotype association signals, 65.74% showed no significant associations at the abundance level (linear regression, Bonferroni-corrected meta-analysis P > 0.05; Fig. 3d,e). To illustrate the added value of SNV associations, we systematically assessed the phenotypic associations with the gut microbiome at the species abundance, SNV and structural variant levels. Among the 62,464 species–phenotype pairs (Methods), 533 showed associations at SNV level, 460 (86.30%) showed associations only at SNV level, and just 5 (0.9%) showed associations at all 3 levels (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Tables 11–13). These results suggest that SNV-based analyses provide complementary information to structural variant- and abundance-based analyses when investigating host–microbiome associations4,5,23.

Among 940 signals, 810 were linked with intrinsic factors and 130 with exposure factors (Supplementary Note 7). We found 152 pairwise signal combinations involving 26 intrinsic phenotypes (excluding age, sex and height), in which the same tag SNVs were associated with 1 or more exposure factors (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Table 14). To assess whether exposure factors confounded the association signals of the intrinsic factors, we included the exposure factors as covariates in a robust association test using LMM-based permutation tests (999 permutations) for the association signals shared between intrinsic phenotypes and exposure factors. Owing to data completeness requirements (phenotype, exposure and SNV all had to be observed in at least 100 samples), we could evaluate 66 signals. Of these, 54 (81.8%) remained significant in at least 2 cohorts after controlling for the exposure factors (permutation P < 0.05), suggesting that the exposure factors did not confound the majority of the SNV associations with intrinsic phenotypes.

Age showed the highest number of association signals (99 signals) involving 8,117 SNVs across 42 species (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11) (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 10). We next assessed how well microbial SNVs could predict host age (Methods). To this end, we trained a machine learning model in the DMP cohort and evaluated its predictive performance in the other cohorts. The model explained 12.8–42.0% of the variation in age (R2) in the test datasets (Supplementary Notes 8 and 9, Supplementary Figs. 8–10 and Supplementary Tables 15 and 16), suggesting the predictive potential of gut microbial genetics for host age.

The most robust signal was supported by four independent cohorts (meta P < 5.42 × 10−11; Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 10). This signal contains five SNVs in the genome of F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274), and their associations were not confounded by other microbial features, including bacterial lineage, species abundance and structural variants (Extended Data Fig. 8 and Supplementary Note 10). Notably, all five age-associated SNVs are missense variants located in the sarA_2 gene (gene ID: 102274_01471). The most significant SNV was 102274_1617247 (effect allele: T, effect allele frequency = 17.38%, β = 4.93, meta-analysis P = 1.00 × 10−17), showing that individuals carrying the T allele were 4.9 ± 0.6 years older (mean ± s.d.) than those without the T allele (Supplementary Table 10). The linkage disequilibrium analysis showed that the lead SNV 102274_1617247 is linked with the other four missense SNVs (R2 > 0.2; Fig. 4a,b) in sarA_2, and significant signals were detected in all cohorts except 300OB (Fig. 4c,d). Notably, all 300OB participants are older than 50 years and show a higher frequency of age-associated alleles compared with the other four Dutch cohorts, which have younger average ages (Extended Data Fig. 9). In other words, the age-associated allele in the sarA_2 gene of F. prausnitzii_I was enriched in an older population. Moreover, replication of the association across the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Fig. 4d) suggests convergent genetic changes during host ageing in different ethnic groups.

The sarA_2 gene is a homologue of the oppA gene, which encodes an oligopeptide-binding lipoprotein with a Tat pathway signal sequence in its N terminus. The protein product of sarA_2 also forms an outer-membrane unit of an ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transporter system responsible for the uptake of oligopeptides—the oligopeptide permease (OPP) complex (Fig. 4b). We thus hypothesized that the age-associated missense SNVs may influence the function of the SarA_2 protein (also known as OppA). To test this, we assembled the OPP complex based on the AlphaFold3 prediction, including the five subunits encoded by sarA, oppB_4, oppC_4, oppD_4 and oppF_4 (Fig. 4e). This structural comparative analysis revealed that the predicted OPP structure is similar to the substrate-binding protein-dependent ABC transporter systems of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8JA7)24 and E. coli (PDB: 6CVL)25, supporting the plausibility of the predicted ABC transporter architecture. The sectional view of the predicted OPP complex structure revealed a tunnel-like cavity, with the OppA subunit acting as a gate for the transportation tunnel (Fig. 4e). Notably, the age-associated SNVs we identify are located in the cavity of OppA that relates to the tunnel (Fig. 4f), which suggests that these SNVs may affect the transportation function of the protein complex.

To infer the potential ligand of the OPP complex and better understand the underlying age-related changes in transport function, we examined the functional annotations of each subunit of the complex in detail. The OppF_4 subunit, encoded by the gene 102274_01467, was annotated as a GsiA subunit of the transporter for glutathione, an antioxidant that can prevent the damage caused by oxidative stress for both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. We then compared the protein sequences of OppA, OppB_4, OppC_4, OppD_4 and OppF_4 with 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system and found that all 5 subunits match existing protein sequences (E-value < 1 × 10−10; Methods), indicating that the OPP complex may function as a glutathione transport system. In silico molecular docking analysis further revealed that glutathione can bind to the pocket region of the OppA protein (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10). This suggests that age-associated mutations may affect glutathione uptake efficiency and help F. prausnitzii_I better resist ageing-related oxidative stress in the intestinal environment.

Motivated by the structural characterization of age-associated SNVs in sarA_2, we further systematically depicted the effect of associated SNVs in relation to protein structures. To this end, we focused on 6,799 associated missense SNVs, which are related to 3,724 proteins. We retrieved high-confidence three-dimensional structures of 2,141 (57.49%) proteins with 3,705 associated missense SNVs from the ESM Metagenomic Atlas26 and AlphaFoldDB27. We then systematically characterized these SNVs in relation to structural properties, including relative solvent accessibility (RSA, how exposed a residue is to a solvent), distance to ligand (DTL, distance from the residue to the nearest predicted pocket centre) and distance to protein–protein interaction interface (DTPPI, distance to the closest residue within a predicted protein–protein interface region) (Methods). We designated SNVs in low-DTPPI regions (DTPPI < 10 Å) or low-DTL regions (DTL < 15 Å) as structurally important28,29,30,31,32. Out of 3,705 SNVs, 752 (20.3%) were structurally important by these criteria, including 246 and 528 SNVs affecting amino acid residues in low-DTL and low-DTPPI regions, respectively (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 17). These SNVs were associated with 40 different phenotypes (Fig. 5b,c).
